w: What's tested Why we mount casts: diagnosis (CR vs MIP mountings), treatment planning, diagnostic waxing, treatment Arcon vs non-arcon; the UAB classification (non-adjustable, semi-adjustable, fully adjustable) Non-adjustable articulators: accurate in one position only, who benefits, mounting without a facebow Semi-adjustable: sagittal condylar inclination and the Bennett angle; the facebow, CR record, MIP record and eccentric records, and the errors each one prevents or causes Fully adjustable: kinematic facebow, pantograph, why record thickness doesn't matter there but does on a semi-adjustable Choosing an articulator: the patient's occlusion, the extent of the work, the instrument's limits, the clinician 1 Articulator size: best value when it is similar in size to the patient; a small hinge costs chair time A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Cheap, quick, small to ship: good for the lab, not for the dentist or the patient. Advantages: low expense and little effort. But that benefits the lab, not the dentist: labs like these because they are quick, inexpensive and small (low shipping costs), and dentists often don't ask for more ("all you have to do is ask"). Because the articulator doesn't replicate the patient, the restoration can't meet the occlusal requirements of the patient's eccentric movements, so the dentist spends chair time adjusting it, and grinding often destroys anatomic contour and leaves poor occlusal relationships (zirconia, which doesn't adjust or polish well, makes this worse). Partial-arch articulators also can't verify the mounting cross-arch or let you model the occlusal form from the opposite side. "There is never an advantage to the dentist for the lab to use this articulator": its hinge axis can be very different from the anatomic one, sometimes directly behind the second molar, and it can't move in pathways like the patient's. Dentists seem to accept that adjusting crowns is normal: "NO!" 2 Non-adjustable articulators: accurate only in MICP, an advantage to the lab, not to you A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank No adjustment can bring a non-adjustable articulator closer to the patient. Its movements range from a hinge only to eccentric movements based on averages. However different they look (a palm-sized hinge, one glued to the back of the cast, one that looks like yours with no adjustments), they are all accurate in only one contact position, MICP. Their opening and closing paths and all their eccentric motions don't reflect the patient. The procedure is an arbitrary mounting in MICP. Any interocclusal record that separates the teeth increases the error, because when it is removed the articulator closes along a different arc from the patient's mandible. The smaller the articulator compared with the patient, the larger that error. 3 Choosing the articulator: anterior teeth need at least a semi-adjustable; the job dictates the tool A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Choose by the patient's guidance and the extent of the work. 1. The patient's occlusion. Anterior guidance usually predominates in eccentric tooth contact, because it is closer to the teeth. With strong anterior guidance, a less sophisticated articulator can be used for posterior teeth (a crown on #20 will disclude). With poor anterior guidance (little vertical or horizontal overlap, malaligned or missing teeth, pathology; skeletal Class II arch discrepancies, edge-to-edge Class III), the posterior determinant controls more of the movement and a more sophisticated articulator is needed. It is hard to justify a non-adjustable articulator for any tooth that is part of the anterior guidance. 2. The extent of the restorative work. The more the articulator mimics the patient, the less intraoral adjustment. Minor procedures can use simpler instruments; complex reconstruction (a four-unit bridge from #22 to #18 replaces half the posterior occlusion) needs more sophisticated ones. "The job dictates the tool, not the other way around." 3. The limits of the articulator system, in how much intraoral adjustment will be needed. 4. The skill of the clinician: "A semi-adjustable articulator in the hands of a knowledgeable clinician may be of greater assistance in treatment than a fully adjustable articulator in the hands of an inexperienced operator" (add to that, a careless one), and if the records are careless or the casts inaccurately mounted, any articulator loses its usefulness. 4 The facebow mounts the maxillary cast only, on a three-point reference plane A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank The facebow mounts the maxillary cast (never the mandibular) in a similar relation to the patient's hinge axis, for function and esthetics. It consists of an ear-bow (caliper), a transfer assembly and a bite plate, and it needs a reference plane defined by three points on the patient that are calibrated to the articulator: two posterior points, usually the auditory canals, which estimate the transverse horizontal hinge axis, and one anterior point, which depends on the system (nasion, orbitale, or a set distance from the edge of the maxillary teeth). The reference plane is usually the Frankfort horizontal (some use Camper's plane). In an indirect mounting only the transfer assembly is attached to the lower member of the articulator to mount the cast, which simplifies mounting and lets the ear-bow stay in the clinic. 5 An arbitrary facebow is close enough (2-5 mm); skipping it risks a cant and mounting errors A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this Skip the facebow and you risk an occlusal cant in the esthetic plane. Without a facebow the instrument loses much of its value. Incorrect maxillary orientation gives an error in the esthetic plane (risk of an occlusal cant: you hesitate to hand the patient the mirror), an error in the occlusal plane (risk of protrusive, non-working and working interferences), possibly incorrect cusp height, and grooves and cusps that don't match the patient. The result is more chairside adjustment, often ablating anatomic form: more work for the dentist to fix, if possible, what was easily avoided. Hinge axis and facebow. The facebow relates the maxilla to both the patient's hinge axis (PHA) and the articulator's hinge axis (AHA). With a kinematic facebow, AHA = PHA; with an arbitrary facebow, AHA is near PHA. Mounting errors show up in protrusion and laterotrusion: a cast mounted too posterior or too superior gives premature or heavy contacts on the most anterior teeth; too anterior or too inferior gives premature or heavy contacts on the most posterior teeth. 6 The MIP record: most common, most misused; hand articulate whenever you can A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Most common, most misused: the second most common cause of lab problems after a bad impression. Use an MIP record only when the casts won't hand-articulate. The lab mounts with whatever you send. VPS MIP records go over the prep only, trimmed to the cusp tips and off soft tissue. It is the most common record and "also the most misused record." The number one cause of lab problems is a bad impression; the second is the mounting, usually from misusing MIP records. The most important rule: hand-articulate the casts whenever you can, and use a registration only if they are unstable. If you send the lab a record, they will mount with it, so don't send one "just in case." If you use VPS: don't cover the occluding surfaces of unprepared teeth (in MIP they are supposed to touch; material over the prep is fine), don't register soft tissue (it moves in the mouth but not in stone), and if missing teeth don't allow a stable mounting, use a record base. Two reasons a registration, whatever the material, rarely fits even when trimmed: the material's resilience, and detail greater than the stone cast's. Occlusion is measured in microns; 20 µm off and the crown is out of occlusion. Used with care, VPS can be very accurate; otherwise it adds error. Trim windows so you can see the cusps seat. 7 VPS MIP records go over the prep only, trimmed off cusp tips and soft tissue A professor's hint · 2 questions in the bank Explained under 6 above: The MIP record: most common, most misused; hand articulate whenever you can 8 Protrusive records are preferred for the SCI: a lateral record reads steeper A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Protrusive records are preferred: the lateral SCI is steeper, the protrusive one keeps restorations discluded. Eccentric records program the articulator to follow the patient's condylar movement. They are most meaningful when mounted in CR (bilateral balanced occlusion in dentures, reorganized treatment). The protrusive record: the mandible moves forward from CR 3-5 mm, without lateral deviation; one record sets the SCI on both sides. Lateral records: the mandible moves in laterotrusion 3-5 mm; you need two (left and right working motion), and each sets the contralateral SCI and the contralateral medial-wall settings (Bennett angle and immediate side shift): a right lateral record sets the left side. Protrusive records are preferred. The SCI measured with a lateral record (down the medial wall) is steeper than the SCI from a protrusive record (down the articular eminence). If the goal is posterior disclusion, contacts that are avoided in protrusion will also miss in right and left laterotrusion, so the shallower protrusive SCI is the safer setting: if the articulator is shallower than the patient, the patient just gets more disclusion; if it is steeper, the restoration may hit. For the same reason many clinicians set an arbitrary 30°: most patients' protrusive angles range from about 20 to 60° (commonly 35-40°), so a 30° setting gives decent anatomy and still discludes in the mouth (20° makes the cusps too shallow). For a bilateral balanced denture you would do the opposite; that comes later. 9 Eccentric records at 3-5 mm: farther out, the Bennett angle reads smaller A professor's hint · 2 questions in the bank Know this Protrusive and lateral records: 3-5 mm. Farther out the Bennett angle reads smaller and the fossae come out narrow. Why 3-5 mm? Beyond that the condyle's path is curving and the teeth are separated anyway. The orbiting condyle's path curves, so the Bennett angle measured depends on where the record is taken: at 3-5 mm of condylar movement the angle is larger; at 7-10 mm it is smaller, which builds narrower fossae on the posterior teeth and more likely interferences. 10 The Bennett angle is the setting he would leave off first; the SCI matters more A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this The Bennett angle is the less commonly adjusted setting; SCI matters more. 2. Bennett angle: in mediotrusion the orbiting condyle moves inward (anterior, inferior and medial), which affects the width of the central fossae of the posterior teeth. It is the angle of that inward path in the horizontal plane relative to a straight protrusive path, set on the medial wall of the fossa. More sophisticated instruments can also set the immediate lateral mandibular translation (immediate side shift, ISS). The Bennett angle is less commonly adjusted: "if I was going to leave any feature off of an articulator, I'd probably leave this one," because the average values are close enough for most general dentistry. 11 CR vs MIP mountings: a CR mounting finds MIP, an MIP mounting can't find CR Core of the slides · 2 questions in the bank Diagnosis. Mounted diagnostic casts improve visualization of the static and functional relationships of the teeth and make it easier to replicate mandibular movement and the contacts it produces. Pathologic contacts often can't be seen clinically, because protective neuromuscular reflexes steer the patient around them, but properly mounted casts show them. A CR mounting is the most useful for diagnosis: it allows the fullest range of movement, so you can evaluate every contact and slide, close into CO (often unstable) and still move into MIP. An MIP mounting can't reposition the condyles to CR, so it can't show the CO contacts. From a CR mounting you can always find MIP; from an MIP mounting you can't get back to CO. Also flagged in class On every objectives slide. A small hinge never follows the patient's arcs. The articulator decides how much you adjust at delivery: chair time is money. Teeth in the anterior guidance need at least a semi-adjustable articulator. Facebow = maxillary cast. CR or MIP records relate the mandibular cast. Arbitrary (ear-canal) bows are within 2-5 mm: clinically insignificant. His closing line: the facebow and the right records pay for themselves at delivery.
